findings.text: `f-arolw-013` names three source paths and not the section's fourth write path, the new test, so a node reading the followup alone would not create the file the done-when measures

findings.reason: it is the interval the prescribed recording point leaves open, and a gate that never exercises it passes whatever the implementation does there.
findings.text: the seven cases include the launcher-alive-past-the-window and the launcher-dead-with-a-recorded-supervisor cases but none where the launcher dies after the supervisor has started and before its pid is written, so the gate cannot show the freeing rule holds across that interval

findings.reason: the recording point cannot produce the invariant the section states, so the node must either persist the pid inside the spawn step (before the survival wait, as the fleet ack file already does) or have the supervisor record its own pid on start, and a case must cover it.
findings.text: the section frees a reservation only when no process of its launch is alive and prescribes recording the supervisor's pid "as soon as `_start_supervisor` returns it", but `_start_supervisor` does not return until `_confirm_supervisor_survived` has waited up to `SUPERVISOR_SURVIVAL_SECONDS` = 2.0 s (dispatch_launch.py:2371, 2390, called at :2721 and :2725), so through that whole interval a live supervisor is unrecorded and a launcher killed there frees the reservation — a second launch is then admitted beside a live supervisor, which is the two-workers-one-worktree defect the section exists to close

findings.reason: the section's own extension of the rule to in-harness doors has no freeing path, so the mechanism as written deadlocks the run on the door it explicitly covers; the rule needs a release at the end of the launch (unwind or completion) with process liveness only as the fallback for a killed launcher.
findings.text: the section extends the reservation to "an in-harness dispatch and a caller-supplied launcher" and then frees it only when no process of its launch is alive, but an in-harness launch is delegated rather than spawned (dispatch.py:3037) and starts no supervisor, so the only process the rule can inspect is the dispatching process — the coordinator or MCP server, which outlives the launch by design — and a failed or completed in-harness launch of an existing run id therefore holds its reservation until that process exits, refusing every later launch of the run with nothing in flight
